Dezeen School Shows: a hotel located in a former railway station in New York City is among the projects from students at Pratt Institute.

Also featured is a wellbeing space that highlights existing water systems and outdoor furniture that create communal spaces in New York City's urban spaces.

Pratt Institute

Institution: School of Design – Interior Design
Course: MFA Interior Design Thesis
Tutors: Alper Besen, Nina Freedman, Frederic Levrat, Irina Schneid and Edwin Zawadzki

School statement:

"The MFA in Interior Design at Pratt Institute prepares students to engage in critical inquiry through theoretical and applied research, establishing them as innovators and leaders in the field of interior design.

"The curriculum addresses emerging and innovative technologies, sustainable practices, interdisciplinary collaboration and issues of ethical and social responsibility in a diverse and global context.

"Seeing the possibility of design as an agent of change, Interior Design at Pratt expands the potential of professional practice, design education and our understanding of the built environment.

"The program culminates in a thesis project developed in the final year of study. Work is done under the direction of a thesis advisor and is completed within one year.

"The thesis provides students the opportunity and freedom to pursue a topic in depth, building on the studies they have undertaken during their time at Pratt."

Transitions of Water and Space: Pathways to Wellbeing by Jenna Alghanim

"This project explores how interior design can support physical and environmental wellbeing through spatial, sensory and material transitions shaped by proximity to water.

"Located at Battery Weed, the design reimagines the historic fort as a restorative threshold, integrating visible water systems to reconnect occupants with ecological processes."

Student: Jenna Alghanim
Tutor: Irina Schneid
Email: jalghan9[at]pratt.edu

Designing the Interior as an Anti-Algorithmic Apparatus: Reclaiming Cognitive Autonomy through Spatial Rhythms in the Digital Age by Chuhui Chen

"Designing the Interior as an Anti-Algorithmic Apparatus reimagines the public library as a civic space for recovering attention in the digital age.

"Set within Levels 5-7 of New York's Stavros Niarchos Foundation Library, the project transforms reading, searching and gathering into a vertical sequence of spatial countermeasures.

"Branching routes, fragmented indexes and debate chambers disrupt predictive information habits. Phone-free reading landscapes slow perception through posture, softness and time.

"Collective installations turn knowledge into shared interpretation. The library becomes a place where visitors are invited to pause, compare and encounter perspectives beyond their own; a civic interior shaped by slowness, agency and presence."

Student: Chuhui Chen
Tutor: Edwin Zawadzki
Email: cchen632[at]pratt.edu

Urban Vernacular Resilience by Ayuti Fathmarany

"How can vernacular architectural principles support the resilience of informal communities in dense urban housing?

"This thesis explores how Indonesian vernacular principles – expressed through community culture, adaptable domestic spatial systems and locally accessible materials – can enhance livability and socio-economic resilience in Jakarta's mixed-use rental public housing."

Student: Ayuti Fathmarany
Tutor: Alper Besen
Email: ayuti.fathmarany[at]gmail.com

Craft as Bridge: Living through Making by Yu He

"Situated on the historic grounds of Manhattan, the project positions Lenape culture as the permanent host framework for rotating global indigenous craft traditions.

"Reframing hospitality as a relationship between host and guest cultures, this thesis explores indigenous craft as cultural display and lived spatial exchange."

Student: Yu He
Tutor: Nina Freedman
Email: yhex79[at]pratt.edu

Night Island by Xin Lan

"Night Island explores how 'darkness' can function as a restorative spatial condition within the overstimulated environment of New York City.

"Located beneath Times Square, the project creates a sequence of spaces that gradually transition users from exposure to withdrawal through reduced light, sound and social intensity.

"Rather than treating darkness as the absence of light, the project investigates its potential to support rest, reflection and sensory recovery.

"Through movement, descent, privacy and controlled atmospheres, Night Island offers a temporary urban refuge where visitors can slow down, disconnect from constant stimulation and reconnect with their own physical and mental rhythms."

Student: Xin Lan
Tutor: Frederic Levrat
Email: rositalan88[at]163.com

Look Closer: A Hidden Underground Installation Revealing the Untold Stories of Blue-Collar Labour by Haley Ho-Kyung Lew

"Transforming the subway, a space of unconscious routine, into moments of awareness.

"The project reveals the overlooked labour of blue-collar workers, inserting quiet interruptions created by voids and cutouts into daily movement to expose what has long remained unseen."

Student: Haley Ho-Kyung Lew
Tutor: Alper Besen
Email: hklew0104[at]gmail.com

Weaving Echoes: Interior Design as a Medium of Cultural Memory in Evolving Urban Contexts by Simin Liu

"This thesis explores the role of interior design in reinforcing spatial and collective memory to mediate cultural erasure and displacement in historic immigrant neighbourhoods that are continuously evolving."

Student: Simin Liu
Tutor: Irina Schneid
Email: design.simin[at]gmail.com

Foraged Interiors by Helen Mohney

"In urban environments where vast landscapes are scarce, foraging encourages connection to nature at an intimate scale – cultivating a spirit of appreciation and stewardship.

"This thesis proposes a community space to engage residents in foraging's edible, medicinal and material possibilities, transforming how we experience nature in the city."

Student: Helen Mohney
Tutors: Nina Freedman
Email: hmohney[at]pratt.edu

Between Boundaries: Reclaiming Urban Boundaries as Pedestrian Threshold Spaces by Jingwen Zhang

"Between Boundaries explores how urban streets can become more inclusive and socially engaging public interiors.

"Focusing on the spaces between sidewalks, storefronts and buildings, the project reimagines rigid architectural edges as adaptable threshold spaces.

"Through a system of movable and responsive urban furniture, boundaries can expand, contract and be reconfigured according to everyday activities such as walking, gathering and resting.

"By blurring conventional distinctions between public and private space, the project proposes a more flexible street environment that encourages occupation, social interaction and a stronger sense of belonging within the city."

Student: Jingwen Zhang
Tutor: Frederic Levrat
Email: jingwenzh402[at]gmail.com

Terminal Hotel by Keliang Li

"Terminal Hotel transforms the Terminal Warehouse into a public-facing 'terminal' where locals, visitors and hotel guests can all arrive, pause and move through restorative experiences together.

"The hotel stay is designed like a travel journey – arrival, lounge, transition and destination – so guests withdraw from the city and let their body and mind 'travel' through atmosphere, wellness, dining and culture.

"As an urban resort in the city centre, it offers a tranquil escape with resort-level amenities while staying deeply connected to New York."

Student: Keliang Li
Tutor: Edwin Zawadzki
Email: klix28[at]pratt.edu

item.content:encoded:
Continuing our Future Stadium series, we take a look at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in London, where Populous aimed to innovate the stadium typology with a multifunctional design that prioritised the fan experience.

The 62,850-seat Tottenham Hotspur Stadium opened in 2019 as the home of Tottenham Hotspur Football Club, built on the site of the team's former stadium, White Hart Lane. Covering an area of 43,000 square metres, it is almost double the size of its predecessor.

As well as hosting the north London football team and its fans, the multipurpose stadium was the first outside the USA to be designed to host NFL games, made possible by a retractable pitch.

The stadium's natural-turf pitch, used for football matches, fully retracts to reveal an artificial playing surface for American football games and music concerts – this is one of the design choices Populous made to make the stadium a sports and entertainment hub that would attract visitors all year round.

"What made the project unique wasn't any single innovation, but the ambition to rethink what a stadium could be," Populous managing director and global head of design Christopher Lee told Dezeen.

"From the outset, the brief wasn't simply to replace White Hart Lane," he continued.

"It was to create a new home for Tottenham Hotspur that felt authentic to the club, its supporters and the local community, while setting a new benchmark for the experience of attending football and live events."

According to Lee, Populous designed the stadium seating as if it were a concert arena, working with acoustic engineers Vanguardia to create an environment that would generate a sense of atmosphere when the bowl is filled with spectators.

"We worked with [Vanguardia] to design the acoustic environment to make it one of the loudest stadiums but also one where reverberation time and acoustic echoes were tuned so songs and chanting would last longer," said Lee.

The seats were designed at the steepest angle allowed by regulations, up to 35 degrees, aiming to bring fans closer to the pitch.

Wrapping the stadium's asymmetric bowl are metal cladding and swathes of glazing, including a protruding glass volume that marks the entrance at the West Stand.

Tall glass facades also hug around the southern end of the stadium, revealing views from the street of two large tree-like columns supporting the 17,500-capacity South Stand, a defining feature of the stadium and the largest single-tier stand in the UK.

Topping the 34-metre-tall South Stand is a glass walkway, where visitors can walk out to touch the cockerel above.

Underneath the iconic stand is The Market, a five-storey-tall glass atrium containing a large food and drinks hall, with a 65-metre bar that stretches the length of the pitch's goal line.

Read:

Ten stadiums of the future that rewrite the playbook

Although there are exclusive spaces at the stadium, named Sky Lounges, Populous purposefully designed The Market as a vibrant hospitality space to be enjoyed by all visitors, regardless of ticket price.

Lee aspired for the stadium to be "a piece of community infrastructure rather than simply a football ground," which, after seven years, has contributed to its enduring legacy.

"Perhaps one of the project's most enduring impacts has been the way it democratised the stadium experience," said Lee.

"Historically, there was a clear distinction between hospitality and general admission, with the better experiences reserved for those paying the highest ticket prices. We wanted to dissolve that traditional hierarchy."

Lee believes the ethos of prioritising the fan experience at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium has impacted the design of stadiums around the world.

"I think that philosophy has had a lasting influence on stadium design," he said. "Increasingly, clubs recognise that the quality of a stadium isn't defined by its most exclusive spaces, but by how successfully it curates a diverse range of experiences for everyone.

"Ultimately, that's what democratising the fan experience means."

When the stadium opened in 2019, Lee described it as "the best stadium in the world" – a belief he still holds today.

"What's interesting is that seven years later, the conversation isn't really about individual features anymore," he said. "It's about the authenticity of the experience, and I think that's why the stadium has endured as a benchmark."

"The project demonstrated that a contemporary stadium can be both globally ambitious and deeply rooted in its local identity. Those two things are often presented as opposites, but they don’t have to be – in Tottenham, they reinforce one another."

"Many of the technical innovations have now been emulated elsewhere, which is exactly what happens with influential projects," Lee continued. "But what is much harder to replicate is the emotional connection people have with the building."

The photography is by Hufton + Crow unless stated.

Future Stadium

This article is part of Future Stadium, our series exploring the growing role of monumental sports buildings in architecture and urbanism around the world.

item.content:encoded:
Recycled plastic tiles that mimic natural slate cloak a dormer extension at this terraced home in London, which has been updated and expanded by local practice YN Studio.

Named Tile House, the Victorian terrace in Hackney was reworked with a contemporary palette of natural and recycled materials, with its darker, tile-clad exterior contrasted internally by linings in Douglas fir.

"The project started from a question about compatibility: whether a contemporary rooftop extension could sit comfortably within a historic Victorian street without resorting to imitation," YN Studio director Alex Smith told Dezeen.

"Rather than mimicking the original building, we looked for materials and moves that could be honest about their newness while remaining genuinely in dialogue with their context," he added.

YN Studio organised the extension around a skylit staircase atop the home's existing stair, creating a generous double-height lobby visible from the home's entrance.

White walls and Douglas fir shelving help to maximise the feeling of space in this stairwell, while an internal window helps to pull natural light and views into the extension's new study space.

"The double-height stair lobby is probably the moment we are proudest of," Smith said.

"In a relatively modest rooftop extension, it would have been easy to maximise every square metre of floor area. Instead, we gave over a significant portion of the plan to a vertical void."

Read:

Will Gamble Architects frames Ribbon House extension with weathered steel

"That decision gives the project its character, and the addition feels spatially generous and architecturally considered rather than a cluster of densely packed rooms," he added.

The main bedroom has been relocated into the new dormer space, where it sits beneath a Douglas fir ceiling with a deep-set skylight at its centre. Douglas fir has also been used for a datum around the room's edge and a bespoke full-height wardrobe.

Opposite, the study has been tucked under the existing roof pitch and furnished with a plywood desk on wheels, and a skylit bathroom is finished with crisp white tiles and a terrazzo floor.

The ground floor layout has been left largely unchanged, with an additional extension clad in quarry tiles planned to start on site later in the year. The studio is also involved in creating an extension for the neighbouring property.

YN Studio was founded by Smith in 2017. Previous projects by the studio include Bradbury Works, a retail and office building in Dalston, which featured a shed-like form clad in an "X-ray" facade of translucent polycarbonate panels.

Another dormer extension recently completed in London is Lewisham Loggias by OEB Architects, which takes cues from Italian palazzos and paintings.

The photography is by French + Tye.

item.content:encoded:
Italian photographer Andrea Ferro has documented the remaining 1950s bubble houses in Dakar, Senegal, as they face increasing threats of demolition.

Ferro decided to document the concrete-dome homes – known as bubble houses due to their construction using inflation – to show their unique forms and offer a glimpse of daily life inside them.

"As a documentary photographer and videographer, I spend a few months each year based in Dakar," Ferro told Dezeen. "I recently discovered this subject with strong architectural and visual potential that immediately inspired me to develop a new, different story."

"My aim was to record the architectural and historical significance of this rare experiment in thin-shell design, and to portray a fragment of everyday life that reveals Dakar's social as well as urban fabric," he continued.

Built from the 1950s through to the 1970s, the houses were informed by a concept developed by American architect Wallace Neff in California.

Each of the homes was built by inflating a dome-shaped balloon, which was then sprayed with cement to form a solid shell. While only a handful of these Airform homes were built in America – all of which have now been demolished – by the 1970s, there were around 1,200 of them in Dakar.

"Post-war Dakar faced a sharp housing shortage under the late-colonial French administration – the city was growing fast, budgets were tight, and new workers needed homes quickly," explained Ferro.

"Neff's Airform domes offered a rare fit – fast to erect, material-light, and climate-savvy for heat and sea winds – so authorities adopted them at scale in sites like Ouakam, Zone B and Hann, creating what became the world's largest concentration with around 1,200 units."

Originally built in groups of 100 to form entire neighbourhoods, many of the houses were demolished as Dakar expanded, while others have been integrated into the city fabric.

The ageing material, along with the current wave of development in the Senegalese capital, means that in recent years, many of the remaining homes have been demolished.

It is estimated that fewer than 100 remain in the city, but the majority of these are still occupied. Ferro was keen to show how they are being used while drawing attention to the fact that they are increasingly under threat.

Trained as architect, Ferro believes that raising awareness of the structures and demonstrating how they could be renovated may increase the chances of some of the bubble houses being saved.

"In Dakar, they became a unique urban experiment: modular, low-cost bioclimatic homes now partially absorbed, altered, or decaying – leaving a fragile, living record of tropical modernism," he said.

Read:

Domed home in California is designed to feel both "ancient and otherworldly"

"They're pressured by land speculation, lack of legal protection, 'obsolete' layouts and services, and marine-climate decay of thin ferro-cement shells – so owners demolish, overbuild, or abandon them," Ferro continued.

"I'm a documentary photographer; meaning I observe and elaborate through images, though, if I imagine possible future strategies to save them – at least some of them – these could be: to list key clusters, publish simple retrofit toolkits and pilot one or two model restorations."

Other recent photography collections published on Dezeen include Johan Blasberg's pictures of Egypt's New Administrative Capital.

item.content:encoded:
Architecture studio Vector Architects has arranged a cluster of art galleries around a preserved Banyan tree canopy near Guangzhou, China.

Developed for Aranya Jiulong Lake, a holiday retreat near Jiulong Lake Reservoir 45 kilometres away from central Guangzhou, the art centre was broken into several free-standing galleries connected by gardens and plazas. According to Vector Architects, the arrangement was designed to be a departure from standard art museums.

"Breaking away from the closed 'white cube' archetype of traditional art museums, Aranya Art Center Guangzhou integrates art openly into the rhythms of daily life," said Vector Architects.

"Art becomes accessible in the midst of mundane moments – a quick walk downstairs, a casual meal, a wait for the community shuttle bus – each an invitation to step into the gallery."

At the centre of the gallery pavilions is the Banyan Tree Avenue, a 50-meter-long canopy of 25 banyan trees running from east to west, which serves as an outdoor venue for public art display and community events.

"Within this coexistence of the old and the new, the site evolves through architectural intervention, while the trees become the tangible embodiment of the site's spirit," said Vector Architects.

An open pavilion featuring an array of columns anchors the west end of the avenue, while the main art hall sits on the east end.

The facade of the main art hall is clad in textured glass bricks on the outside and translucent polycarbonate panels on the inside, to allow natural light in while maintain climate boundary.

Three three-standing galleries were located along the north side of the Banyan tree avenue, interwoven by preserved trees and a walking path covered by a continuous overhanging eaves extended from the gallery buildings.

The combination of indoor and outdoor spaces was designed to respond to south China's hot, humid and raining climate.

The south side of the tree-covered avenue is defined by meandering corridors with various viewing platforms set among the tree canopies, creating the viewing experience of a Chinese garden.

The corridors eventually lead to the final gallery located at the far southeast of the site. It features a warm-toned concrete ceiling, which slopes down from both ends and meet at the centre, creating a gentle wave form.

Read:

Vector Architects funnels light to forest spa with tubular concrete lightwells

High side windows filter light and cast tree shadows on the undulating ceiling.

A community canteen is located on the northwest side of the site, that can be accessed by one entrance facing the gallery cluster and the other facing the main street used by the local community.

Cantilevered roofs wrap the entire building, encircled by a double-height arcade that provides a sheltered communal space for the neighbourhood.

The open-plan canteen-style dining area occupies the ground floor, with outdoor seating available on the open plaza. Private dining rooms can be found on the first floor.

Vector Architects has built a series of projects for retreat brand Aranya at various cities across China. Recent examples include Wulingshan Eye Stone Spring spa with tubular concrete lightwells and the monolithic Chapel of Music.

item.content:encoded:
Architecture studio Ortega Diago has transformed part of a warehouse in San Sebastian, Spain, into a locker room and changing facility for more than 100 factory workers.

The studio founded by Gonzalo Sánchez Ortega and Armando Diago was approached to design the changing rooms in a long, narrow space at one end of a factory.

Every day, the facility needed to serve more than 100 employees of a company operating in the mobility technology sector, with distinct areas for male and female staff.

The existing building was inefficiently organised, so Ortega Diago introduced a series of freestanding walls with varying heights that restructure the space while allowing daylight to pass above and around them.

"The main objective was to maximise the amount of natural light within the interior," the architects told Dezeen.

"From the outset, we knew that the vertical partitions had to allow light to pass through while simultaneously concealing the changing areas from the circulation spaces."

The staggered geometric volumes obscure sightlines where privacy is required, while creating clear, unobstructed circulation routes without completely enclosing the spaces.

According to the architects, the most challenging aspect of the project was reorganising the elongated space, with access at only one end, in a way that could accommodate a high volume of traffic.

"The corridor – both inevitable and exceptionally long – ultimately became the element that made this new spatial organisation possible and one of the intervention's most distinctive features," they pointed out.

A pared-back material palette, including granite, wood and steel, lends the spaces a utilitarian, Brutalist aesthetic that matches the industrial context.

The architects say they used materiality to "establish hierarchy and order among the partitions", choosing to work exclusively with tone and texture rather than colour or decoration.

Read:

Eight homes in former factories that echo their industrial past

Granite is used as a unifying element across the flooring, partitions and doorways, with honed and bush-hammered finishes adding texture.

The stone is complemented by the use of satin-finished stainless steel for the locker fronts. This metal produces gentle reflections that amplify light and movement within the space.

A plinth that supports the lockers is made from board-marked concrete that introduces a tactile detail, while stained hardwood doors provide a warmer tone.

The use of simple etched numbers on the locker fronts exemplifies the project's focus on formal restraint and a rigorously minimalist approach.

In the washroom area, a row of wall-hung ceramic basins with exposed traps is supported by slender chrome legs. Flush-mounted mirrors and sconces with exposed bulbs contribute to the pared-back, industrial feel.

A window at the far end of the locker room provides a view of the greenery outside, allowing nature and daylight to connect the serene interior spaces with the outdoors.

Other recent renovations of industrial buildings include Schemata Architects' transformation of a former ironworks into a cafe and brewery, as well as the conversion of a 19th-century factory in New York into a vast hotel.

The photography is by David Zarzoso.

Dezeen School Shows: a proposal to reimagine the historic Japanese port town of Tomonoura is among the projects from the Singapore University of Technology and Design.

Also featured is a project exploring care infrastructure for residents living within Manila North Cemetery and an ecological masterplan for Singapore's coastline.

Singapore University of Technology and Design

Institution: Singapore University of Technology and Design
School: Architecture and Sustainable Design (ASD)
Course: Master of Architecture
Tutor: Frederick Peter Ortner

School statement:

"The Master of Architecture programme at the Architecture and Sustainable Design (ASD) pillar represents the deep investigation into the technology and research-infused design pursued by SUTD.

"This is an accelerated course held over three terms, principally comprising practice, studio and thesis elements.

"It is designed to orientate and focus students through a longer-term thesis-based design methodology and project; and to realise new visions of novel creative and social design futures."

Caretaking: Care Infrastructures in the City of the Dead by Aceson Han

"Metro Manila's fragmented urban landscape exposes the limits of formal planning in addressing inequality, access and environmental threats.

"Nowhere is this more visible than in Manila North Cemetery, one of the city's last remaining plots of green space and home to generations of residents who sustain its daily operations as grave caretakers, builders and service providers.

"This thesis argues that the everyday practices of caretaking within the cemetery already function as a form of urban stewardship.

"Rather than treating informality as a condition to be removed, the project proposes spatial and infrastructural strategies that strengthen existing systems of care, labour and community organisation."

Student: Aceson Han
Course: Thesis
Tutor: Calvin Chua
Email: aceson_han[at]mymail.sutd.edu.sg

Towards a New Oceania: Manifestations of Extraction and Survival by Darius Chen

"To speak of the Pacific Islands is already to speak in a colonial tongue: small, scattered, peripheral to a Euro-American centre. This thesis rejects that cartography, aligning instead with Hau'ofa's Our Sea of Islands.

"On Kiritimati, extraction and survival have long been told as one story, with phosphate, nuclear testing and rising sea levels rendering Pacific peoples as victims to be saved or resources to be tallied.

"The design response operates across scales – component, dwelling, settlement and atoll – facilitated by a digital twin built for planning under deep uncertainty.

"Through stochastic agglomeration, components and infrastructure emerge as relational assemblages, creating an architecture of vā through which Oceania authors its own futures."

Student: Darius Chen
Course: Thesis
Tutor: Eva Maria Castro
Email: darius_chen[at]mymail.sutd.edu.sg

Chthulucene Manifesto by Adelin Johari

"Amidst the global environmental crisis, biodiversity stands as the final and most crucial planetary system at the brink of collapse.

"Environmental destruction remains rooted in a human-centric worldview, where human needs are prioritised over forms of life on the planet.

"This necessitates an urgent rethinking of how we relate to the environment, motivated by the concept of 'decentring' proposed in Donna Haraway's Chthulucene.

"The thesis challenges existing global systems concerning ecological sustainability and conservation, and speculates on living within a damaged planet through designing multi-species, symbiotic relationships.

"Design is explored in spatialising alternate forms of communicating, co-producing, co-consuming and co-existing with 'more-than-humans'."

Student: Adelin Johari
Course: Thesis
Tutor: Eva Maria Castro
Email: adelin_johari[at]alumni.sutd.edu.sg

Diet Town: Towards a Rural Degrowth Metabolism by Jonathan Leong Zhen Cong

"Diet Towns proposes a rethinking of architecture's role in rural Japan, shrinking faster than it can repair itself.

"Centred on the Shinetsu region – Japan's deep-winter interior, where climate, culture and demographic decline converge – the thesis reframes decline not as a pathology to be reversed but as a material condition to be spatialised.

"Instead, Diet Towns advances a territorial theory of degrowth: the deliberate withdrawal of settlement footprint, the deconstruction of surplus buildings as a new form of material production, and the return of land to forest, water and low-maintenance ecologies.

"Iiyama is positioned as the prototype town where governance, material flows and commons-based land management can be reorganised through a Degrowth Co-Op."

Student: Jonathan Leong Zhen Cong
Course: Thesis
Tutor: Calvin Chua
Email: jonathan_leong[at]mymail.sutd.edu.sg

Where She Thrives by Paraaga Raghavendra

"Across India, women are systematically excluded from the spaces that shape everyday life. Confined behind thresholds and restricted by social and spatial barriers, many are left with limited access to work, safety, visibility and autonomy.

"Public streets remain hostile, workplaces distant, and homes rarely empowering.

"The thesis explores how architecture can reconfigure these conditions by working within the existing fabric of the city. Rather than singular interventions, it reconnects domestic, economic and social systems to support new forms of collective life.

"The project works across multiple layers. Thresholds are reconfigured to connect women through shared systems of care and labour."

Student: Paraaga Raghavendra
Course: Thesis
Tutor: Calvin Chua
Email: paraaga_raghavendra[at]alumni.sutd.edu.sg

Pelagic Territories by Yiew Jae Tzen

"Sovereignty in the South China Sea, tethered to fossil fuels and military control, undermines itself as environmental degradation renders land-based authority untenable.

"As vanishing territories displace millions, governance must pivot from territorial enclosure towards decentralised maritime infrastructures, establishing regional commons sustained by collective labour that reframe political authority in an ocean that inherently resists enclosure.

"This fluid sovereignty integrates China's decarbonisation goals with ASEAN's labour capacities through green ammonia for energy and circular aquaculture for food security."

Student: Yiew Jae Tzen
Course: Thesis
Tutor: Eva Maria Castro
Email: jaetzen_yiew[at]mymail.sutd.edu.sg

(Re)Settling the East Coast: A Bolder and Better Long Island Plan by Chua Shuei Ray Eusebius

"Singapore's coastal developmental projects have historically prioritised monetary value, built functionality and shoreline security in their design, from its early colonial days to the present time. This has resulted in an engineered and 'grey' coastline that has destroyed and displaced shoreline ecology.

"As a result, Singapore is losing more and more of its marine coastal ecological heritage in the name of 'progress'.

"Despite concerns for the environment only recently entering the design of built spaces, a surprising amount of Singapore's flora and fauna have survived and resettled the 'grey' coastlines of Singapore.

"This project proposes that by centring the design of reclaimed land around the principle of ecological connectivity, coastal ecologies can be incorporated instead of displaced from the urban fabric."

Student: Chua Shuei Ray Eusebius
Course: Thesis
Tutor: Stylianos Dritsas
Email: eusebius_chua[at]mymail.sutd.edu.sg

A Porous Belonging by James Tan Shi An

"Situated on Ōshima Island, a former Hansen's disease sanatorium in Japan, this thesis investigates how architecture can transform landscapes of isolation into environments of belonging, care and renewal.

"Historically shaped by segregation, surveillance and social stigma, the island embodies spatio-temporal fractures that severed relationships between individuals, communities and everyday life.

"Rather than erasing this history, the project reinterprets it through the concept of porous belonging, positioning architecture as a mediator between autonomy and care.

"A regenerative mental wellness campus emerges through the adaptive reuse of former sanatorium structures and graduated conditions of ecological, social and sensory porosity."

Student: James Tan Shi An
Course: Thesis
Tutor: Frederick Peter Ortner
Email: james_tanshian[at]mymail.sutd.edu.sg

[Home]eostasis by Austin Law

"'All Watch Over by Machines of Loving Grace.' Written by Richard Brautigan in 1967, the poem imagines a future in which humans and machines coexist within a mutually supportive ecology, where technology quietly cares for and responds to human needs. Nearly six decades later, our homes remain far from this vision.

"[Home]eostasis is a speculative housing project that reimagines the home as a living system capable of continuously adapting to its occupants throughout their lives.

"The proposal envisions a feedback loop between occupants and their environment, supported by artificial intelligence.

"Spaces are able to transform in response to changing household requirements, while lighting, airflow, acoustics and access are continuously calibrated to support occupant wellbeing."

Student: Austin Law
Course: Thesis
Tutor: Sam Conrad Joyce
Email: austin_law[at]alumni.sutd.edu.sg

Memory Re-Formed by Aye Yu Mon

"Memory Re-Formed explores artificial intelligence as a creative design methodology for architectural regeneration.

"Rather than treating AI as an autonomous image generator, it positions AI as a collaborative design tool, guided through critical judgement, curated datasets and iterative experimentation, to reinterpret the collective memory embedded within historic places.

"Using the historic port town of Tomonoura, Japan, as a case study, the project develops an AI-assisted workflow that combines heritage analysis, diffusion models and computational modelling.

"The resulting proposal extends Tomonoura's streetscape into the Seto Inland Sea through a series of floating and fixed structures that function simultaneously as public space, cultural infrastructure and marine habitat."

Student: Aye Yu Mon
Course: Thesis
Tutors: Erwin Viray and Frederick Peter Ortner
Email: yumon_aye[at]mymail.sutd.edu.sg

item.content:encoded:
Brazilian studio Suite Arquitetos has used Portinari ceramic tiles to create a residential-style show space during Casacor São Paulo 2026.

Based on the event's theme Mind and Heart, Suite Arquitetos designed Casa Magma as a space to present various Portinari tiles – as well as Brazilian furniture and art – during the exhibition hosted at Parque da Água Branca.

The 215-square-metre "suite" installation was organised around a central living room, which forms the "heart" of the project.

This is accessed via an entryway defined by a sweeping wall clad in fluted tiles, which guides visitors into the hub.

Dark red, walnut, burgundy and terracotta tones appear continually throughout the space, creating a warm, enveloping aesthetic.

"The space was born from this desire to create a contemporary shelter, almost like a cocoon," said Suite Arquitetos. "We wanted people to feel the environment even before rationally understanding it."

"Casa Magma speaks about welcoming and about this silent power that exists in matter, light, and textures," it continued.

A sunken living area revolves around an exposed column that's treated to resemble a fireplace, with a cylindrical base filled with logs.

Arc-shaped, velvet-upholstered sofas at either end of the sunken area form dual seating areas around original furniture, all united by a plush rust-toned carpet.

The curved entry partition also features fluted tiles on its concave side, and sweeps around the space to draw the eye from end to end.

At its zenith, a small kitchen and bar sits below a sculptural light fixture comprising natural crystals and tubes by Suite Arquitetos, while mid-century chairs by Joaquim Terneiro accompany the counter.

Read:

Studio Melina Romano gets creative with fibreboard at Casa Alma in São Paulo

Figurative artworks include a Diego Rivera drawing and an Odoardo Tabacchi sculpture, while more abstract pieces range from a metallic stool by Rodrigo Zampol to a relief panel by Zanini de Zanine.

In a minimalist bathroom, textured Portinari ceramic tiles are highlighted by soft recessed lighting and complemented by matte brown fixtures.

"Applied to walls and floors, the stone expands the tactile reading of the environment and highlights different customization possibilities," said the team.

During previous editions of Casacor São Paulo, Studio Melissa Romano got creative with fibreboard for an installation titled Casa Alma in 2021 and Studio Arthur Casas designed a prefabricated home in 2018.

Early work by Suite Arquitetos includes a restaurant featuring upside-down plant pots, bare lightbulbs and exposed ductwork.

The photography is by Pedro Ocanhas.

Casacor São Paulo runs from 2 June to 9 August 2026 in São Paulo, Brazil. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

item.content:encoded:
Japanese studio Kenta Sano & Associates has completed a four-storey building in Tokyo that that has a glass-fronted dance studio on its lower floors and a house on top.

Designed for owners who ran a ballet school from their previous home, the building replaces an ageing semi-basement space with a purpose-built studio with a 4.2-metre ceiling for dancer's lifts and jumps.

It was topped with a residence on the upper floors.

Viewed from the street, Tokyo Ballet House contains three stacked elements.

An open ground floor with parking and back-of-house spaces for the school, the contemporary, glass-fronted dance studio and the more traditional home.

The full-height glazed facade reveals ballet rehearsals to passersby in what the architects describe as "an antithesis to the conventional model of the urban dance studio".

"Dance studios, including ballet studios, are often closed spaces because privacy is prioritised," principal architect Kenta Sano told Dezeen.

"In contrast, we proposed a studio that opens boldly toward the city as an antithesis to this conventional model of the urban dance studio."

"The space allows the energy of practice to become visible as part of everyday urban life," he continued.

"If the north-facing opening is imagined as a proscenium and the textile as a stage curtain, the studio becomes a stage, while the city outside expands like audience seating."

While the north elevation of the building was enclosed with glazing, the opaque west facade was clad in ribbed expanded polystyrene (EPS) panels.

More commonly used as insulation, the EPS boards were cut into trapezoidal sections to create deep vertical fins that cast changing shadows across the exterior.

Inside, exposed steel beams and services are left visible above mirrored walls, while a sprung linoleum floor laid over a cushioned subfloor was incorporated to provide a balance of softness and slip-resistance needed for dancers.

Read:

Glenn Howells Architects creates lantern-like school for English National Ballet

Above the studio sits a smaller residential volume occupying the third and fourth floors, surrounded by planted terraces.

The gaps between the stacked volumes create deep eaves, while trees and shrubs line the terraces around the home.

The building occupies a corner site in Toshima, close to Rikugien garden, in a long-established residential neighbourhood where increasing redevelopment has gradually reduced the area's greenery.

In response, the architects introduced trees and planting around the home and along the pavement edge.

According to the studio, the landscaping references the neighbourhood's history as one of Edo's largest nursery districts while introducing more greenery into an area undergoing redevelopment.

Inside the home, a simple layout places the bedroom above a box containing bathrooms and storage, leaving the remaining floor as an open-plan living, dining and kitchen space beneath a sloping roof.

Oak flooring continues from the living spaces onto the surrounding timber terraces, extending the main living areas outdoors.

According to Sano, opening the studio to the neighbourhood has had an unexpected impact since the building was completed.

"One of the most rewarding outcomes was seeing the activities within the studio become widely recognised by the local community," he said.

"After the new studio was completed, a woman in her nineties who lives nearby joined the ballet school as a new student."

Founded in Tokyo, Kenta Sano & Associates designs houses, cultural buildings and public projects across Japan.

Other dance studios featured on Dezeen include the lantern-like English National Ballet by Glenn Howells Architects and a light-filled dance centre in California by LOHA designed to reflect the "ephemeral nature of performance."

The photography is courtesy of Kenta Sano & Associates.

The next World Cup will be unlike any previous, with more stadiums on show than ever

item.content:encoded:
With the 2026 FIFA World Cup reaching its conclusion and in keeping with our Future Stadium series, we've rounded up all the stadiums set to host matches at the 2030 World Cup, which will be played across three continents.

The next World Cup will be unlike any previous, with more stadiums on show than ever before.

Eleven venues in Spain are expected to host matches at the tournament, as well as six in Morocco and three in Portugal.

In addition, Uruguay, Argentina and Paraguay will each host one of the three opening games in honour of the centenary of the inaugural World Cup, held in Uruguay in 1930.

Read:

File into the Future Stadium

Four of the 23 stadiums will be entirely new, with 11 undergoing renovations ahead of the tournament – including some major overhauls. Of the eight stadiums not set to have any major works before 2030, most were either constructed or renovated within the past decade.

Several common themes emerge among the ongoing projects, highlighting current trends in stadium architecture.

These include moves to bring stands closer to the pitch, the addition of roofs, the introduction of VIP areas and "hospitality zones", adaptability measures to enable the venues to host cultural events as well as sports, and the integration of LEDs into the facades.

Read on to find out more:

Camp Nou, Barcelona, Spain

Opened in 1957, FC Barcelona's iconic home ground is in the midst of a €1.5 billion renovation led by Japanese architecture firm Nikken Sekkei in collaboration with Spanish architecture studios IDOM and B720 Fermín Vázquez Arquitectos.

It will see the Camp Nou expanded to become the largest stadium in Europe with a capacity of 105,000 seats.

Work began in 2023 and is currently targeting a 2027 completion, though the project has faced some delays.

The final phase involves the addition of a new roof that will collect rainwater to irrigate the pitch, and will require the team to temporarily move out of the stadium for a second time during construction.

Gran Canaria Stadium, Las Palmas, Spain

International architecture studio L35 Architects is working with Madrid-based firm Estudio 0710 on an overhaul of Gran Canaria Stadium, which first opened in 2003 and is home to Las Palmas.

The ongoing project is titled La Nube – The Cloud – and will feature the addition of a continuous membrane roof structure.

Capacity will also increase from 32,000 to more than 44,000.

Estadio La Cartuja, Seville, Spain

Originally built as an athletics venue in 1999, La Cartuja was designed by Spanish architecture firm Cruz y Ortiz Arquitectos.

The studio is currently leading a two-phase remodelling of the building set to complete in 2028, which has already increased its capacity to become Spain's third-largest stadium with 71,000 seats.

As well as an expansion of the stands, the project will include the removal of the athletics track, the addition of a glass roof over the stands, and a modernisation of the facade.

Metropolitano Stadium, Madrid, Spain

Cruz y Ortiz Arquitectos was also responsible for the Metropolitano Stadium, originally completed in 1993 as an athletics venue.

Following an extensive rebuild that took its capacity from 20,000 to 70,000, it became the home of Atlético Madrid football club in 2017.

Nueva Romareda, Zaragoza, Spain

Nueva Romareda will replace Real Zaragoza's original La Romareda stadium, which stood on the same site and was demolished in 2024.

Designed by IDOM, the new stadium is planned to open in 2027 with a capacity of 43,000.

According to the studio, its form was heavily influenced by Zaragoza's famously strong winds, with concave elevations to the north and south and convex to the east and west.

Anoeta, San Sebastián, Spain

Anoeta is the home stadium of Real Sociedad. First constructed in 1993, it underwent a redevelopment overseen by local studio Izaskun Larzabal Arquitectura that completed in 2019.

The project saw the removal of a running track to move fans closer to the pitch, an increase in capacity to 40,000 seats and the addition of a translucent blue ETFE skin around the exterior.

Following the rebuild, the stadium beat Tottenham Hotspur Stadium and the Puskás Aréna to win the sports architecture category at the prestigious Prix Versailles in 2020.

RCDE Stadium, Barcelona, Spain

Spanish studio Fenwick Iribarren Architects, which worked on multiple venues for the 2022 Qatar World Cup, collaborated with Barcelona-based studio Gasulla Arquitectura Integral on the design of RCDE Stadium, completed in 2009.

Located on the outskirts of Barcelona, it serves as the home of RCD Espanyol and has a capacity of 40,000.

Notable architectural features include a roof covered in photovoltaic panels and a translucent curtain wall finished in the team's colours, which illuminates at night.

San Mamés, Bilbao, Spain

Another IDOM project, the 53,000-seater San Mamés stadium was completed in 2013 for Athletic Bilbao.

The building's facade is made up of more than 2,700 identical louvres, giving it a variable appearance depending on the viewing angle.

At night, the facade can be lit up in solid colours or to display moving graphics.

Santiago Bernabéu, Madrid, Spain

Real Madrid's fortress of a home ground completed a major renovation in 2024, designed by German firm GMP Architekten in collaboration with L35 and Ribas & Ribas.

As well as increasing its capacity to 83,000, it saw the structure's concrete exterior wrapped in sinuous steel louvres.

Other changes included the addition of a retractable roof and a literally groundbreaking system for separating the pitch into six sections and storing them across six underground levels.

Nou Mestalla, Valencia, Spain (not yet confirmed)

Fenwick Iribarren Architects has designed a replacement for Valencia CF's legendary Mestalla Stadium.

The project has been decades in the making, with construction begun on a different architect's design in 2007 but halted two years later due to financial issues at the club.

Building recommenced per Fenwick Iribarren Architects's design in early 2025, and is expected to complete in 2027.

The new 70,000-seater stadium will have a retractable membrane roof and a building envelope defined by what the studio describes as "a series of flowing, open promenades that connect with the city".

Football's global governing body is currently considering a proposal for the stadium to be a venue at the tournament, with a final decision expected in late 2026.

Balaídos Stadium, Vigo, Spain (not yet confirmed)

Originally opened in 1928, the home of Celta Vigo has undergone multiple renovations over the years, most recently between 2015 and 2021.

This major modernisation project saw the structure sheathed in shimmering metal fronds, designed by local architecture and engineering firm Capitel.

However, to be eligible to host games at the 2030 World Cup, the Balaídos's capacity will need to be significantly expanded in order to meet FIFA's 40,000-seat requirement.

As with the Nou Mestalla, FIFA is expected to make a decision on the stadium's involvement at the 2030 World Cup later this year.

Adrar Stadium, Agadir, Morocco

Originally conceived as part of the planning for Morocco's failed 2006 FIFA World Cup bid and then revived as part of its failed 2010 bid, Adrar Stadium was completed in 2013 and will now, after almost 25 years, host World Cup football.

Designed by Italian studio Gregotti Associati International and Moroccan architect Sâd Benkirane, the unique stadium appears to be embedded in the ground. The seating bowl is entirely surrounded by a stepped pyramid clad in orange stone that was informed by the surrounding hills.

The first stage of a renovation was completed ahead of the African Cup of Nations in 2025, with a giant roof structure planned ahead of the 2030 World Cup as the second phase in the stadium's upgrade.

Grand Stade Hassan II, Casablanca, Morocco

Sports architecture juggernaut Populous is working with Moroccan architecture studio Oualalou + Choi on a brand new stadium being constructed specifically for the 2030 World Cup around 40 kilometres outside Casablanca.

Named after the former king of Morocco, it is planned to have 115,000 seats, which would make it the world's largest football stadium.

The stadium will sit below a giant tented roof – a reference to traditional Moroccan cultural festivals known as moussem.

It is currently competing with the Santiago Bernabéu to host the World Cup final in 2030, with no venue yet confirmed.

Fez Stadium, Fez, Morocco

Opened in 2007, Fez Stadium is the oldest facility in Morocco set to host games at the upcoming World Cup. Designed by state-owned National Society for the Management and Rehabilitation of Stadiums, the 35,000-seat stadium has a pragmatic form distinguished by four inward-leaning, concrete flood-light towers.

The stadium opened with a playing surface surrounded by an athletics track. A renovation led by French studio BMF Architects updated the stadium ahead of the African Cup of Nations in 2015, and – like many of the stadiums in Morocco – there are plans to remove the running track ahead of the World Cup.

The second phase of the renovation will also see the entire stadium wrapped in a new facade.

Grand Stade de Marrakech, Marrakesh, Morocco

Mother stadium designed by Italian studio Gregotti Associati International and Moroccan architect Sâd Benkirane, the 45,000-seat Grand Stade de Marrakech was opened in 2011 as the city's main football venue.

With a distinctive square form that bears a striking resemblance to Stadio Luigi Ferraris in Genoa, also by Gregotti Associati International, the stadium has the distinction of being the world's only rectangular stadium to include a running track. One key criticism of this arrangement is that it pushes many spectators far away from the pitch.

The stadium was renovated ahead of the 2025 African Cup of Nations and further planned works before the World Cup will see the running track removed and stands reconfigured.

Prince Moulay Abdellah Stadium, Rabat, Morocco

Built on the site of a previous stadium with the same name, the 69,000-capacity Prince Moulay Abdellah Stadium opened in September 2025 after a construction time of just two years.

Now the home of the Moroccan national football team, it hosted the opening game and final of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations.

Designed by Populous, its parametrically designed facade is made up of 19,2000 champagne-coloured aluminium triangles, intended to be a reference both to the interlaced palm leaves that line Rabat's boulevards and traditional Moroccan embroidery.

After sundown, the facade transforms into a giant animated screen thanks to a huge array of LED pixels.

Ibn Batouta Stadium, Tangier, Morocco

Also known as Tangier Grand Stadium, Ibn Batouta Stadium was designed by Moroccan studio JK Architecture as the home of the national football team.

The concrete stadium opened in 2011 with a capacity of 45,000, but was designed to be expanded with both end sections of the round bowl only built up to the first tier. In 2022, upper tiers were added to these sections, increasing the capacity to 65,000 and making it the country's biggest stadium at the time.

A recent overhaul to the stadium by Cabinet Anouar Amaoui has seen the capacity increased again to 75,000 by removing the athletics track and lowering the pitch level to allow for another tier of seating. This renovation also saw the entire stadium clad in a unifying facade and a lightweight PTFE roof added.

Estádio da Luz, Lisbon, Portugal

Populous is working with Lisbon studio Saraiva + Associados on an update to SL Benfica's stadium in the Portuguese capital.

Populous designed the original 68,000-seater stadium, which opened in 2004 and was the site of Portugal's shock defeat to Greece in the UEFA European Championships final that year.

The renovation will take its capacity to 80,000, with the stands reshaped to bring fans closer to the pitch and the introduction of safe standing and premium hospitality areas. On the outside, there will be a new programmable LED facade.

As well as changes to the stadium, work is underway on a regeneration of the surrounding site, with the masterplan including a new 10,000-capacity indoor arena, a swimming pool, a theatre and events space, two indoor sports halls, a rooftop football pitch and running track, a large new fan plaza, and commercial and residential buildings.

Estádio José Alvalade, Lisbon, Portugal

Just three kilometres from Estádio da Luz, Estádio José Alvalade is the home of top-tier side Sporting CP. It was designed by Portuguese architect Tomás Taveira in the early 2000s as one of three new stadiums he designed to host games at Euro 2004.

The 52,000-seat stadium is topped with a roof supported by four 60-metre-high masts. Originally bright yellow to match the brightly coloured patchwork facade, both been changed to club-colour green in recent years.

Ahead of the 2030 World Cup, the stadium has been undergoing a series of renovations led by Fenwick Iribarren Architects to increase capacity and improve facilities. The first stage of this renovation, which recently completed, saw the removal of a moat around the pitch and the reconfiguring of the stands to move spectators closer to the action.

Estádio do Dragão, Porto, Portugal

Designed by Portuguese architect Manuel Salgado, FC Porto's home stadium has a capacity of 50,000 people.

It was inaugurated in November 2003 with a friendly match against Barcelona, in which a 16-year-old Lionel Messi made his professional debut.

The club has been carrying out modernisation work on some of the stadium's amenities, and in February announced that it had start evaluating the "future intervention needs" of the polycarbonate roof, which is supported above the stands with two huge lattice arches spanning 178 metres.

Estadio Centenario, Montevideo, Uruguay

As part of the celebrations to mark the tournament's 100th birthday, the opening match of the 2030 World Cup will be hosted at the Estadio Centenario in Montevideo.

Fittingly named – although centenario refers to the 100th anniversary of the Uruguayan constitution not the World Cup – the stadium was built in 1930 for the inaugural tournament where it hosted 10 games, including the final.

Built within a year, the reinforced-concrete stadium was designed by Uruguayan architect Juan Antonio Scasso. It consists of four curved, multi-tier stands that together form a bowl along with a distinctive 100-metre-high tower, which is accessed from the football museum within the main stand. Perhaps uniquely in world football, this stand also includes a primary school.

The stadium has undergone several renovations, but its form and structure remain largely as they were in 1930 and in recognition of its significance to world football, Estadio Centenario was declared the first, and only, Historical Monument of World Football by FIFA in 1983.

Current plans to renovate the stadium ahead of the World Cup by SB Arquitectos and Vigliecca & Asociados include replacing a stand, lowering the pitch level and adding a roof.

Monumental Stadium, Buenos Aires, Argentina

River Plate's home ground, the Monumental Stadium, will host the second match of the 2030 World Cup.

German firm Schlaich Bergermann Partner is working with Brazilian studio Fernandes / Arquitetos Associados on an expansion of the stadium that will see it become one of the world's largest, increasing capacity from 85,000 to 101,000.

The project includes the introduction of a new standalone upper tier of seating around the entire bowl, as well as a new roof.

Osvaldo Domínguez Dibb Stadium, Asunción, Paraguay

As part of the World Cup centenary celebrations, Paraguay will play its opening match on home soil in a brand new stadium.

The intended venue is the Osvaldo Domínguez Dibb Stadium, currently under construction in Asunción. It will replace Club Olimpia's previous home ground on the same site, demolished in 2025.

Designed by Argentinian architecture studio Path Urban and Nicole Hellmers Arquitectura, the 46,000-seater new stadium will be Paraguay's largest.

Some reports have raised concerns about whether the project will be ready in time, with the initial target completion date of 2027 now pushed back to 2029 amid construction delays. Meanwhile, the stadium has undergone a dramatic redesign from the original vision unveiled in 2024.

Additional reporting by Tom Ravenscroft.

Future Stadium

This article is part of Future Stadium, our series exploring the growing role of monumental sports buildings in architecture and urbanism around the world.

item.content:encoded:
Australian interiors studio YSG has converted a historic warehouse in Sydney into a modern co-working space.

Located in the inner-city suburb of Redfern, the 387-square-metre corner property was built in the early 1900s and until recently, housed an art gallery with adjoining residential quarters.

Its owner, who hails from Cape Town, named the project Cinderella House after a late 19th-century South African gold mine that promised life-changing wealth to contemporary pioneers.

Drawing on the open skies of South Africa and his travels through southern Texas, the client wanted the space brightened by colour and light.

"Our client is originally from Cape Town and has an affinity for southern Texas," YSG director Yasmine Ghoniem told Dezeen.

"He wanted the space to blend open blue skies and sandy deserts, relieving the residential levels of their austere minimalism," she continued.

As a result, the stark white walls and black detailing of the original interiors have been replaced with layers of texture, pattern and colour informed by Mojave design.

With the ground floor out of the studio's remit, Cinderella House spans three levels starting from the first floor.

Members enter through a side entrance leading to a mezzanine fitted with co-working desks, before a stairway extends up to the main social sub.

The nucleus of the business, this floor houses a kitchen, dining and living room, along with a central courtyard and a meeting room with an attached balcony.

The original interiors were gutted. Walls once painted white are now lined with wood panelling, while a textured hemp render flecked with straw covers the courtyard.

Southern Texan country themes run through each space via bold patterned rugs, geometric Mojave designs and carefully arranged vintage furniture.

"We incorporated upholstered vintage armchairs and cushions with tessellated rectangular grids and woven stripes," said Ghoniem.

"The zebra grains on the blonde birch wall panels and the darker swirling burl veneers offset these symmetrical patterns."

Agave greens, apricot oranges and sandy browns come through the rugs of the meeting room and living area, while stepped Mojave elements recur across textiles, window treatments and timber joinery fronts.

"Some favourite features are our custom rugs that reference high desert landscapes," said Ghoniem. "We tapped into the patchwork quilt designs of Folk Fibers in Texas, applying more energising colours."

Read:

Berlin co-working space offers "more than a boring desk"

New steel doors replaced old ones, and to counterbalance the otherwise angular decor of the interiors, they were studded with decorative baubles.

To achieve a similar effect, hand-beaten timber rafters were slotted into the living room ceiling with woven raffia cladding fitted between each one.

Green and black tiles bridge indoor and outdoor spaces, running from the living room into the courtyard and up a yellow-tiled seating platform topped with a large potted cactus.

Glass garage-style doors provide access to the courtyard, opening the space up fully during warmer months and bringing the sky into the main social hub.

Upstairs, a more intimate, enclosed lounge is housed, equipped with a Murphy bed for overnight guests. This lounge leads to the client's personal office through a corridor.

The corridor was lined with coloured portholes inspired by Perspex sculptures his by wife, artist Anna Dudek. A large circular window in the private office frames views of the sky.

The office also features a walk-in bar connected to a drinking ledge that extends onto a patio as a set-up for hosting colleagues. The existing deck was repaired rather than replaced.

"My favourite outdoor feature is the deck on the top floor," said Ghoniem. "We patched the rotten planks, sealing them in a creamy clay tone that we then accentuated with orange and brown stripes, aligning with the Mojave motifs inside."

The bathrooms were remodelled, with one in a deep terracotta red and another with a floating vanity carved from Opus Rosso marble.

"The space certainly feels like a residence more than an office, especially on the kitchen's level," she said. "That's the point of the space, to encourage all the members of the co-working space to exchange ideas over casual gatherings.

Other interiors recently completed by YSG Studio include a holiday home near the New South Wales coast, an office for Australian fashion brand Alémais in Sydney and the Superfreak cafe in Sydney's Marrickville suburb.

The photography is by Anson Smart.

item.content:encoded:
Architecture studio OMA has designed a "jewel box" restaurant clad in cork inside its recently completed extension to the New Museum in Manhattan.

All-day bar and restaurant Oberon has opened a few months after the expansion, which OMA New York completed adjacent to the original SANAA-designed building.

Sitting adjacent to the lobby, in the expansion's ground floor, the 2,500-square-foot (230-square-metre) restaurant appears as a metallic box with a single horizontal band of frosted glass wrapping its exterior, hinting at what's inside. It was clad in cork that was then painted a silver colour, blending it into the industrial materials of the museum s[ace

"'Hidden-in-plain-sight,' the restaurant resembles a jewel box or an inverted white cube gallery," said OMA.

The studio's first restaurant design in the US, Oberon is accessible directly from the museum lobby as well as a separate, speakeasy-style entrance from Freeman Alley.

"We imagined the restaurant both as part of, and independent from the museum," said OMA New York partner Shohei Shigematsu. "Conceived as a freestanding box inserted into the ground-floor lobby, it will be accessible from the building's front and back, day to night."

The interior's moody, cavernous aesthetic is a stark contrast to the museum's industrial concrete and metal lobby and galleries.

"Inside, a large dining room and fixed pockets of seating will offer space to gather or retreat," said Shigematsu. "Organic, tactile material finishes complementing the museum's polished lightness, will introduce a warm and comforting environment that eases people in and invites them to stay."

Over the central dining area, filled with freestanding wooden tables and chairs, the cork ceiling is carved away to create an elongated dome ringed with cove lighting.

Around the restaurant perimeter, each booth sits below its own scooped metallic-coated ceiling element, from which a single pendant lamp by Minjae Kim descends to illuminate the tabletops.

Tropical plants fill the open tops of the booths, casting silhouettes and shadows on the frosted glass that can be subtly traced from outside.

Both the booth seats and the ceiling are formed entirely from black expanded cork, creating a homogenous appearance throughout the compact space.

Read:

OMA completes "highly connected, but highly individual" expansion of New York's New Museum

"The restaurant uses a novel sustainable material which gives a rich softness counter to the museum's white box galleries," said project architect Jake Forster.

"Produced in blocks by heating cork offcuts to a high temperature, the cork self-bonds by its natural resins creating an innovative material that can be cut and shaped."

"A product mainly used for insulation – we have embraced its qualities, carving an intimate and hidden cavern, a new communal space, embedded within the museum," he added.

An interactive digital artwork by Ian Cheng is displayed behind the bar, which is bookended by metal-grate partitions connected by a reflective ceiling.

Elsewhere in the city, Office of Tangible Space recently renovated the interiors of the Brooklyn Museum Cafe, while other new restaurants include a Japanese-influenced spot next to the Stonewall Inn and the revamped dining venues at The Edge.

OMA other recent news includes the completion of the pyramidal Hangzhou Prism in China and the creation an incubator for mushroom production at Fundación Casa Wabi in Mexico.

The photography is by Alex Fradkin.

item.content:encoded:
Dezeen School Shows: the reimagining of a former seaside thermal power plant north of Barcelona set out in painterly visualisations is among projects by Elisava students.

Also included is a series of furniture characterised by the use of taut cables and a modular system of ceramic and wood objects designed for use in urban micro apartments.

Elisava

Institution: Elisava
School: School of Design and Engineering
Courses: Bachelor in Design and Innovation and Undergraduate Degree in Design and Engineering

School statement:

"The Bachelor in Design and Innovation at Elisava trains designers with a creative profile, making them able to apply critical thinking and an exploratory vision of the world to projects, and making them capable of questioning and dialoguing across disciplines with other people from wider social, production, scientific or cultural environments.

"With this bachelor, students can specialise in graphic design, product design, space design or interactive experiences design.

"The Bachelor in Industrial Design Engineering trains students to be design engineers and product developers with a marked transdisciplinary profile, able to conceptualise, design, develop and produce a product, system or service that brings value to industry, society and the planet we live on.

"The Elisava Grad Show brings together every year more than 500 final degree projects from students of the Bachelor in Design and the Bachelor in Industrial Design Engineering, alongside the master's and postgraduate programmes.

"This celebration of final projects at Elisava unfolds as a collective narrative, offering a wide range of stories to explore and share with the city of Barcelona during a programme of events and activities.

"The exhibition features projects developed in collaboration with companies, NGOs, studios, research centres, cultural organisations, institutions and Elisava Research, as well as independent personal work.

"As part of Elisava's 65th anniversary, this year's grad show takes on a special significance by returning to the city centre.

"The aim was to open up the school to Barcelona, bringing design closer to citizens and connecting directly with the vibrant context of La Rambla.

"By situating the exhibition in such a central location, Elisava sought to share the work of the students with a wider audience, reinforcing the dialogue between design, the city and its people."

USM Haller-T by Mateo Prado

"Haller-T proposes an additional layer – not a correction, not a crutch: an extension of the language.

"Through a system of cables and tensioners, the project introduces tension as a force that complements the compression that defines USM. The same structural logic, but in the opposite direction.

"The result is configurations that were not possible within the system: cantilevers, suspended elements, long spans, or an explicit connection between the furniture and its surroundings.

"Haller-T does not invent a new system: it demonstrates that the existing system contained, within its own logic, the exact space where tension could be introduced."

Student: Mateo Prado
Course: Design and Innovation
Tutors: Luis Eslava and German Ortiz
Email: mateucho.04[at]gmail.com

Sobre Com Perforar Una Frontera (O Com Fer Un Colador) by Sol Claret

"Through the figure of the colander and its relationship to the hole and the Mescladís kitchen, this project explores how an everyday object can be transformed into a tool for thinking about the relationship between borders and coexistence.

"The colander thus ceases to be merely a kitchen utensil and becomes a material and symbolic device capable of filtering, connecting and generating new forms of relationship.

"The research begins with the hole and the act of perforating as a response to opaque and delimiting structures.

"The project takes shape through a series of workshops and collective practices developed in collaboration with Mescladís, where manual gestures are approached as practices of experimentation, permeabilisation and openness."

Student: Sol Claret
Course: Design and Innovation
Tutors: Danae Esparza and Guim Espelt
Email: solclaretmuxart[at]gmail.com

L'Acústica Del Jo by Jordina Cascante Riberès

"I open my eyes and, in front of the mirror, I observe a body that I know and yet find unfamiliar. I move closer slowly, wondering who I am, and I realise that I am everything I do not know.

"Then, within the tissues, I discover a set of vibrations passing through me. Suddenly, I return to the mirror, where a body reveals itself to me – one that has ceased to be an image, a body that possesses sonic matter.

"This project emerges from the need to understand my relationship with my own sound and how it shapes my identity.

"Through the body, objects and technology, I explore the possibility of listening to myself from another place, transforming my body into an instrument, material and sonic space."

Student: Jordina Cascante Riberès
Course: Design and Innovation
Tutor: Saúl Baeza
Email: jordinacascante[at]gmail.com

Corpus—liber by Carlos Nogales Alcázar

"This project asks what makes the book unique and why, despite technological progress, it has not been replaced.

"Its permanence does not depend only on its function, but on the physical, symbolic and sensory relationship it establishes with human beings.

"In an age shaped by the internet and artificial intelligence, the book becomes an object of refuge that invites pause, presence and attention.

"Its materiality turns reading into a bodily and ritual experience through gesture, touch, rhythm, weight and smell.

"Organised into five photographic movements, the project visualises the bond between body and book and the qualities that keep it present today."

Student: Carlos Nogales Alcázar
Course: Design and Innovation
Tutor: Rocío Hidalgo Fraile
Email: carlos.nogaless[at]gmail.com

ROCE. Intimidad Como Estructura Del Deseo Aprendido Entre Mujeres by Nara Fusté

"This final degree project explores how social norms become inscribed in the body and manifest through everyday gestures, such as the way we touch, occupy space or relate to others.

"The project challenges the idea that relationships between women exist outside normative structures, proposing instead that they are also shaped by a cultural and emotional inheritance that influences roles, behaviours and relational dynamics.

"Through sequencing, materiality and the dialogue between archive, photography and text, it uses editorial design and the photobook as tools to create a narrative and visual experience in which the tensions of intimacy are made visible."

Student: Nara Fusté
Course: Design and Innovation
Tutor: Pau Llavador
Email: narafustecampos[at]gmail.com

Node. Del Paisatge Resilient Al Land Art by Laura Sun Casellas Sanz

"Node is born from an artistic approach that explores conceptual landscaping, Land Art and the design of ephemeral spaces.

"Rooted in the memory and nostalgia of an oriental landscape, the proposal brings the essence of Asian scenery to transform the waterfront of Les Tres Xemeneies.

"The project falls within the framework of the Catalunya Media City plan, located at the current Turbine Hall.

"The intervention consists of two parts that complement each other: a modification of the site's topography and a temporary, low-impact installation creating new spaces for connectivity."

Student: Laura Sun Casellas Sanz
Course: Design and Innovation
Tutor: Daria De Seta
Email: lucasellassanz[at]gmail.com

Allign. Smart Hanging System by Albert Clariana Llobet

"Allign is an intelligent system integrated into premium retail furniture that automatically repositions garments to maintain uniform spacing between hangers.

"Developed from the observation of visual disorder caused by customer interaction in fashion stores, the solution is seamlessly embedded within a standard clothing rail.

"By combining industrial design, mechanical engineering, electronics and automation, Allign preserves the store's aesthetic quality, enhances brand perception and reduces repetitive staff tasks through invisible automation."

Student: Albert Clariana Llobet
Course: Industrial Design Engineering
Tutor: Xavier Riudor Buscà
Email: albert.clariana04[at]gmail.com

Arquitectura modular per a bombes de calor by Teo Guri

"This project develops a new modular structure for GasN2's industrial heat pumps.

"The proposal transforms a custom-built system into a repeatable, scalable architecture that is easier to assemble.

"Based on folded sheet-metal components and mechanical joints, the system reduces complexity, improves control over the production process and lowers structural costs compared to the previous model.

"The result is an industrialisable platform, validated through a full-scale prototype, that allows future machines to be adapted without having to redesign them from scratch."

Student: Teo Guri
Course: Industrial Design Engineering
Tutor: Alberto Ibáñez
Email: teo[at]guri.cat

L'Ombra. Refugi Climàtic Al Raval by Berta Bigas

"L'Ombra is a modular urban device designed to create spaces for shade, play and social interaction in the Raval neighbourhood.

"The project responds to the climate emergency through a sustainable and replicable proposal that integrates solar energy generation, areas for rest and recreational activities, while encouraging citizen participation and the collective use of public space.

"The project was developed with the participation of CCCB, La Traginera and Elisava, and in collaboration with organisations and companies including Pla de Barris, Persiana Barcelona, and SUD Renovables."

Student: Berta Bigas
Course: Industrial Design Engineering
Tutors: Maria Charneco and Danae Esparza
Email: bertabigassilvestre2[at]gmail.com

Doomo: Modular Ceramic System for Compact Urban Living by Mariona Almuni

"Doomo is a modular ceramic system for compact urban living, developed in collaboration with BD Barcelona.

"Two slip-cast stoneware modules and a wood top that become a side table, stool, umbrella stand, fruit bowl or plant pot depending on the day and the need.

"One object, five lives, one small apartment. Conceived for design-literate urban dwellers.

"A system that reconfigures as life does, building a relationship between user and object that makes replacement feel unthinkable.

"The most sustainable object is the one worth keeping, worth moving and worth passing on."

Student: Mariona Almuni
Course: Industrial Design Engineering
Tutors: Cristina Taverner and Otto Canalda
Email: marionaalmuni[at]gmail.com
